24827.etyen:
From Middle Low German wes, genitive of wat (“what”).
The Low German genitive was often used in subject or object function in the sense of “that which” or “whatever.” For example: Wes deme koninge dunket got, dat is billich dat men also dot. (“Whatever seems good to the king, it is appropriate that one does so.”) Since such a phrase can easily be reinterpreted as “if it seems good to the king”, the Scandinavian conjunction may have developed from this usage.

1004027.etyen:
From Late Latin ablūtiō (“washing, cleansing, ablution”), from abluō (“to wash off, cleanse”), from both ab- (“from, away from, off”), from ab (“from, away from, on, in”), from Proto-Italic *ab, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”), and from lavō (“to wash, bathe; wet, moisten”), from Proto-Italic *lawāō, from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).
Cognate with English ablution, French ablution, Italian abluzione, Portuguese ablução and Spanish ablución.

Compare the parallel formations Danish dobbeltkokosnød, Swedish dubbelkokosnöt and German Doppelkokosnuss (“double coconut”).
